Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Annual WISP review and board report due each Q4 board cycle; state adoption-law changes tracked continuously so new jurisdictions enter the variance appendix within 60 days of enactment

checklist.step: Confirm which legal entities and jurisdictions the law reaches this year
actions: Pull the current writing-company register from the Corporate Secretary with each company's licensed states and NAIC co-codes.
Cross the license list against the tracked register of the 44 jurisdictions that have adopted NAIC Model 668 and mark each company/state pair in scope or out.

Test the small-licensee exemption per state (commonly fewer than 10 employees, including independent contractors) against the HR headcount from Workday and record the result — the incident-notification duty survives most exemptions, so note that on the row.
Record the scoping conclusion per legal entity in Archer GRC and route it to the CISO for acknowledgement.
checklist.done: every writing company has a per-state applicability row in Archer with an exemption test result and CISO acknowledgement.

checklist.step: Refresh the inventory of nonpublic information and the systems that hold it
actions: Query the data catalog for assets classified under the three Model 668 Section 3 nonpublic-information classes: business-sensitive information, consumer personal information (name plus SSN, driver's license, account, biometric) and consumer health information.
Join the classified assets to the CMDB application records so every system storing or transmitting nonpublic information is listed with its owner.
Ask each system owner to confirm or correct the classification within 10 business days and chase non-responders through their department head.
Publish the reconciled inventory to Archer GRC as the WISP scope baseline and date-stamp it.
checklist.done: the nonpublic-information system inventory is owner-confirmed, dated and loaded into Archer as the WISP scope.

checklist.step: Designate the responsible program owner and the security governance committee
actions: Record in the WISP the Section 4(c)(1) designation: the CISO (or named designee, affiliate or third-party service provider) is responsible for the information security program.
Charter the security governance committee with named members from IT Security, Risk, Compliance, Privacy and Legal, meeting at least quarterly.
File the signed designation memo and committee charter in the compliance evidence repository.
Notify the Chief Risk Officer and General Counsel of the designation in writing.
checklist.done: a signed designation and committee charter exist and are referenced in the WISP text.

checklist.step: Anchor the program on the current risk assessment
actions: Open the most recent enterprise cybersecurity risk assessment (REG-052-C02 output) in Archer and confirm it is less than 12 months old.
Map each top-rated risk to the WISP safeguard section that mitigates it and record the mapping in the Archer control library.
Where a rated risk has no mitigating safeguard, raise a program gap to the CISO with a proposed WISP change.
Cite the risk assessment version and date inside the WISP so an examiner can trace program design back to Section 4(c)(2).
checklist.done: every top-rated risk maps to a WISP safeguard or an open, CISO-owned gap, and the WISP cites the assessment version.

checklist.step: Draft or update the WISP against every Section 4 required element
actions: Open the WISP master document in the SharePoint policy library under a new draft version with tracked changes.

Walk the Model 668 Section 4(d) safeguard list — access controls, physical security, encryption of nonpublic information in transit and at rest, secure development, MFA, monitoring, audit trails, secure disposal, testing — and confirm each has a current WISP section naming the operating control and its owner.
Update the incident-response cross-reference to the current IR plan version (REG-052-C04) and the third-party oversight cross-reference to the TPSP program (REG-052-C06).
Route the draft to IT Security Manager, Privacy Officer and Regulatory Counsel for a 10-business-day review and resolve every comment before approval.
checklist.done: a reviewed WISP draft covers every Section 4(d) safeguard with a named control and owner, plus current IR and TPSP cross-references.

checklist.step: Maintain the per-state variance appendix across the 44 adopting jurisdictions
actions: For each adopting state, record in the regulatory tracker the deviations from the model: notification window (72 hours in most states, shorter in some), consumer-count notification threshold, certification requirement and due date, and exemption thresholds.
Subscribe to NAIC and state DOI bulletin feeds and log any new adoption or amendment within 10 business days of publication.
Push confirmed variances into the WISP appendix and notify the Incident Response Lead and Compliance Manager of any notification-window change the same week.
Re-verify the full appendix against current statute text once a year during the WISP review.
checklist.done: the variance appendix lists every adopting state with its notification window, thresholds and certification duty, verified within 12 months.

checklist.step: Approve the WISP through executive management
actions: Present the redlined WISP and the risk-assessment linkage to the executive security governance committee.
Capture approval signatures from the CISO and the Chief Operating Officer (or delegated executive) via DocuSign on the final version page.
Publish the approved version to the SharePoint policy library, retire the prior version to archive, and update the version register in Archer.
Record the approval date as the anchor for the next 12-month review clock.
checklist.done: the approved, signed WISP is published, the prior version archived and the next review date set 12 months out.

checklist.step: Deliver the annual written report to the board per Section 4(e)
actions: Draft the annual report covering the Section 4(e) content: overall program status, material matters (risk assessment results, third-party arrangements, testing results, cybersecurity events and management response) and remediation of identified deficiencies.
Load the report to the board portal ahead of the Q4 risk-committee sitting and brief the committee in person.
Ask the Corporate Secretary to minute the presentation and capture any board direction as action items.
File the report and the minute extract in the compliance evidence repository — this is primary examination evidence of board oversight.
checklist.done: the board report is delivered, minuted and filed with the minute extract for the year.

checklist.step: Publish security policies and train the in-scope workforce
actions: Load the annual security-awareness curriculum (WISP obligations, phishing, nonpublic-information handling, incident reporting duty) into Cornerstone LMS and assign it to all employees and in-scope contractors from the Workday feed.
Set the completion window at 30 days with automatic weekly reminders and manager escalation at day 21.
Chase the residual non-completers through HR Business Partners until completion reaches at least 95%, and report the final rate to the CISO.
Export the completion report and file it in the compliance evidence repository under the training evidence folder.
checklist.done: training completion is at or above 95% with the exported completion report filed.

checklist.step: Align the supporting policy set to the WISP
actions: List the child policies the WISP relies on — access control, encryption and key management, secure development, data retention and disposal, remote work, acceptable use — with their owners and last-review dates.
Flag any child policy older than 12 months or contradicting the WISP and assign the owner a 30-day refresh.
Verify each refreshed policy names the operating systems it governs so examiners can trace policy to practice.
Update the policy register in Archer with new review dates.
checklist.done: every child policy is under 12 months old, consistent with the WISP and registered with owner and review date.

checklist.step: Run the trigger-event review loop between annual cycles
actions: Define the trigger list in Archer: material acquisition or divestiture, new line of business, major system migration, material cybersecurity event, or a new state adoption of Model 668.
When a trigger fires, open a WISP interim-review task within 5 business days and assess which sections need amendment.
Route any amendment through the same executive approval path as the annual review.
Log no-change conclusions too, so the examiner sees the trigger was assessed.
checklist.done: every fired trigger has a dated interim-review task with an amendment or a documented no-change conclusion.

checklist.step: File the program evidence for the retention period
actions: Move the approved WISP, designation memo, board pack, minute extract, training report and variance appendix into the compliance evidence repository under REG-052-C01/<year>.
Apply a minimum 5-year retention label so records survive system migrations and personnel changes.
Verify the repository index retrieves the set by year and by state within one search.
Confirm access is restricted to Security, Compliance, Legal and Internal Audit.
checklist.done: the year's program evidence set is filed, labelled for 5-year retention and retrievable by year and state.

checklist.step: Log and disposition program deviations
actions: Raise a GRC exception for any deviation found during the year: missed review date, unapproved policy in circulation, training below threshold, or a Section 4 element without an operating control.
Assign each exception a root cause, an owner, a compensating control where risk persists, and a remediation date.
Review open exceptions at the quarterly security governance committee and escalate any item older than 90 days to the CISO.
Close exceptions only with attached remediation evidence.
checklist.done: every deviation has a tracked exception with root cause, owner, remediation date and evidence at closure.

checklist.step: Sweep for new-state adoptions and fold them into the program
actions: Each quarter, compare the NAIC's Model 668 adoption map against the tracker's 44-jurisdiction register and identify newly enacted or amended state acts.

For each new adoption where the company holds a license, open a gap assessment covering effective date, transition periods (WISP compliance and TPSP compliance often phase in a year apart) and any certification duty.
Hand the gap assessment to the Security GRC Analyst to update the variance appendix and scoping rows before the state's effective date.
Brief the Compliance Manager so examination readiness includes the new state.
checklist.done: no adopted state where the company is licensed is missing from the register, and each new adoption has a pre-effective-date gap assessment.

checklist.step: Close the annual cycle with CISO remediation sign-off
actions: Review the year-end exception register and the annual test results (REG-052-C01 testing) with the Compliance Officer.
Sign the remediation closure for each resolved deviation and set expectations and dates for any carry-over item.
Confirm the program is ready to support the February 15 certification (REG-052-C05) or direct the documentation of areas requiring improvement.
File the signed year-end review memo in the compliance evidence repository.
checklist.done: a signed year-end memo closes or carries over every exception and states certification readiness.

testing.step: Build the element matrix that defines the test population
actions: Enumerate every requirement of Model 668 Sections 4(a) through 4(i) into a test matrix — one row per required element (risk-based program, designated owner, safeguard list items, board oversight, TPSP oversight cross-reference, IR plan cross-reference, certification support).
Add one row per adopting state for the variance appendix so state-specific deviations are individually testable.
Freeze the matrix and record its source (model act text plus the tracker's 44-state register) in the workpaper.
testing.done: a frozen matrix lists every Section 4 element and every adopting state as discrete test rows.

testing.step: Reconcile the WISP scope to the independent system inventory
actions: Extract from the CMDB all applications flagged as storing or transmitting nonpublic information and compare the list to the WISP scope baseline in Archer.
Investigate every system present in the CMDB but absent from the WISP scope, and vice versa, with the Data Governance Lead.
Treat any nonpublic-information system missing from program scope as an exception, not a reconciliation note.
testing.done: the CMDB and WISP scope agree or every difference is dispositioned as an exception.

testing.step: Re-verify the state-variance appendix against current statute text
actions: Select the domiciliary state plus 9 randomly chosen adopting states (seeded, reproducible selection recorded in the workpaper).
For each, read the state's current Insurance Data Security Act text from the state legislature or DOI site and independently note the notification window, consumer threshold and certification duty.
Compare against the appendix; any stale or wrong entry is an exception, including a correct rule with a superseded citation.
Capture the source page for each state into the workpaper.
testing.done: 10 states are independently re-verified with captured sources and differences logged as exceptions.

testing.step: Verify board oversight actually happened
actions: Pull the Q4 risk-committee agenda, the CISO's annual report and the minute extract from the board portal.
Confirm the report covers Section 4(e) content — program status, material matters, cybersecurity events and remediation — and that the minutes record its presentation.
Check the report date falls within the tested year and trace any board-directed action item to a tracked task.
testing.done: the annual board report, its minuted presentation and any resulting actions are evidenced for the year.

testing.step: Test approval currency and authority on the WISP and child policies
actions: Open the current WISP version and confirm the DocuSign approval is dated within 12 months and signed by the CISO plus the delegated executive.
Sample 8 child policies from the policy register and check each was reviewed within 12 months and does not contradict the WISP.
Confirm the archived prior WISP version is retrievable, proving version control works.
testing.done: the WISP and all sampled child policies show in-date, authorized approvals with working version history.

testing.step: Trace workforce training completions
actions: Reconcile the LMS assignment population to the Workday active-headcount extract as of the campaign launch date.
Recompute the completion rate from raw LMS records and compare to the reported 95%+ figure.
Sample 25 employees across departments and verify each has a dated completion record; sample 5 joiners hired mid-year and confirm onboarding assignment.
Any un-assigned in-scope population segment is an exception.
testing.done: the recomputed completion rate is evidenced and sampled individual records confirm assignment and completion.

testing.step: Re-perform the safeguard-to-control mapping on a sample
actions: Select 10 Section 4(d) safeguards from the matrix, including MFA, encryption at rest, audit trails and secure disposal.
For each, follow the WISP's named control into Archer and inspect one piece of period operating evidence (config export, log sample, disposal certificate).
Reach an independent conclusion on whether the control genuinely operates the safeguard before reading the program's own assessment.
A safeguard mapped to a control with no operating evidence is an exception.
testing.done: 10 sampled safeguards trace to controls with inspected period evidence and an independent conclusion each.

testing.step: Recompute the review-clock and trigger-review discipline
actions: Recompute the months between the last two WISP approvals and confirm the interval does not exceed 12.

List the year's trigger events (material incidents from the ITSM register, M&A activity from Corporate Development, new state adoptions from the tracker) and check each has a dated interim-review task.
A trigger with no assessed review — even a no-change one — is an exception.
testing.done: the approval interval is within 12 months and every identified trigger shows an assessed review.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one GRC issue per test exception with the element or state affected, the evidence gap and the compliance impact.
Assign root cause (scope miss, stale appendix, control not operating, training gap) and a named owner with a remediation date.
Flag any exception that undermines the February 15 certification to the CISO immediately, since certifying over a known material gap is itself a violation.
Carry open exceptions into next year's test as mandatory retest rows.
testing.done: every exception is tracked with root cause, owner, date, certification-impact flag and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, sign and report the program test
actions: Compute the fail count against the thresholds (any unmapped safeguard, stale approval, missing board report, or sub-95% training is a fail).
Write the conclusion — effective / effective with exceptions / ineffective — with workpaper references behind each statement.
Sign as the independent reviewer, having authored none of the WISP content, and file the workpaper in the compliance evidence repository under REG-052-C01/<year>/test.
Report the conclusion to the audit committee and copy the CISO ahead of the certification cycle.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion and committee reporting date is filed in the evidence repository.

checklist.step: Open the annual assessment and fix its scope
actions: Launch the assessment workflow in Archer 120 days before the Q4 board reporting date and assign workstream owners.

Pull the full application list from the CMDB filtered to systems storing or transmitting nonpublic information, plus supporting infrastructure and the Tier 1 third parties from the TPSP register (REG-052-C06).
Document any exclusion (decommissioned system, out-of-scope entity) with a written rationale on the scoping page — silent exclusions are findings in their own right.
Have the IT Security Manager countersign the scope before scoring starts.
checklist.done: a countersigned scope lists every nonpublic-information system and Tier 1 vendor, with rationale on every exclusion.

checklist.step: Catalogue reasonably foreseeable internal and external threats
actions: Build the threat catalogue per Section 4(c)(1): external (ransomware, phishing, credential stuffing, supply-chain compromise) and internal (privileged misuse, accidental disclosure, departing-employee exfiltration).
Pull the year's incident and alert statistics from Splunk to ground each threat in observed frequency.
Fold in sector intelligence (FS-ISAC advisories, state DOI cybersecurity bulletins) and mark threats trending up.
Deliver the catalogue to the Security GRC Analyst as the scoring input.
checklist.done: a threat catalogue grounded in SIEM statistics and sector intelligence covers internal and external threat classes.

checklist.step: Score likelihood and impact for each threat/asset pairing
actions: For each in-scope system, score each applicable threat on the approved 5x5 scale — likelihood from observed frequency and exposure, impact from the sensitivity and volume of nonpublic information held (per Section 4(c)(2), potential damage including to consumers).
Record the scoring rationale on each risk row so the number can be reproduced by a reviewer.
Hold a calibration session with the IT Security Manager and Enterprise Risk Manager to challenge outlier scores before the register is frozen.
Freeze the scored register and version-stamp it in Archer.
checklist.done: every threat/asset pairing carries a reproducible 5x5 score with rationale, calibrated and frozen in Archer.

checklist.step: Assess the sufficiency of existing safeguards against each rated risk
actions: For each risk scored medium or above, evaluate the mitigating safeguards per Section 4(c)(3) across employee training, information systems and threat detection/prevention/response.
Rate residual risk after controls and mark each safeguard sufficient, partially sufficient or insufficient with a one-line justification.
Route every insufficient rating into the remediation pipeline as a finding.
Reconcile safeguard ratings against the control evidence in the REG-052-C03 control program so paper and practice agree.
checklist.done: each medium-or-above risk has a residual rating, a safeguard-sufficiency call and, where insufficient, an opened finding.

checklist.step: Run authenticated vulnerability scans across the in-scope estate
actions: In the scanner console, verify the scan groups cover every in-scope subnet and cloud account from the assessment scope, and schedule authenticated scans.
Export the severity-ranked findings report (CVSS with the internal criticality overlay) and reconcile scanned-asset counts to the CMDB scope list.
Flag any in-scope asset the scanner never touched as a coverage gap on the assessment.
Hand the export to the Security GRC Analyst as scoring evidence and file it in the evidence repository.
checklist.done: authenticated scan results cover the scoped estate, coverage gaps are flagged and the export is filed.

checklist.step: Commission and review the annual penetration test
actions: Agree the rules of engagement with the CISO: external perimeter, one internal scenario and one social-engineering exercise, scoped to systems holding nonpublic information.
Execute the test window with SOC notification so detection performance is measured, not just prevention.
Write findings with reproduction steps, severity and affected nonpublic-information exposure, and debrief the IT Security Manager within 10 business days of test end.
Register each finding in Archer as a remediation item with the standard SLA by severity.
checklist.done: the penetration test report is delivered, debriefed and every finding is registered with an SLA-dated remediation item.

checklist.step: Consolidate the assessment report and risk-rank the findings
actions: Assemble the report: methodology, scope, threat catalogue, scored register, safeguard-sufficiency conclusions, scan and pen-test summaries and the top-10 risk narrative.
Rank all findings by residual risk and tag each with its remediation SLA (critical 30 days, high 90, medium 180).
Circulate the draft to the IT Security Manager and Enterprise Risk Manager for challenge and log their comments and resolutions.
Issue the final report with a version stamp and file it in the compliance evidence repository.
checklist.done: a challenged, version-stamped assessment report with ranked, SLA-tagged findings is issued and filed.

checklist.step: Build the remediation plan with named owners and dates
actions: Convert each finding into an ITSM remediation ticket linked to its Archer risk row, with a named engineering owner and a due date computed from the SLA.
For fixes needing budget or vendor work, record the dependency and get the funding decision minuted at the security governance committee.
Publish the full plan to the CISO with the count of items by severity and due month.
Refuse unowned items — every ticket must carry a person, not a team.
checklist.done: every finding has a linked ticket with a named owner and an SLA-derived due date, and the plan is published to the CISO.

checklist.step: Track remediation to closure and retest fixes
actions: Run the weekly overdue report from the ITSM tracker and chase owners at T-14 and T-3 days before due.
On claimed closure, rescan the asset (or re-perform the pen-test reproduction step) and attach the clean result to the ticket before it may close.
Escalate any critical item past 30 days to the CISO the same day with the exposure summary.
Update the Archer risk row's residual score once the fix is verified.
checklist.done: closures carry retest evidence, overdue criticals are escalated same-day and residual scores reflect verified fixes.

checklist.step: Process risk acceptances for findings that will not be fixed
actions: For any finding proposed for acceptance, require a written business rationale, the compensating controls in place and an expiry date no more than 12 months out.
Route the acceptance to the CISO for signature (critical/high) or the IT Security Manager (medium), and countersign as the second line.
Register the acceptance in Archer against the risk row so it surfaces in the board report and the certification support file.
Diarise the expiry so the acceptance is re-argued, not silently renewed.
checklist.done: every unremediated finding has a signed, countersigned, expiry-dated acceptance registered in Archer.

checklist.step: Feed assessment results into the WISP and control baseline
actions: Hand the top-risk narrative and safeguard-sufficiency conclusions to the WISP owner (REG-052-C01) as the Section 4(c)(2) design input.
Flag to the IT Security Manager any control-baseline change the results demand (new MFA scope, encryption gap, monitoring blind spot) for the REG-052-C03 program.
Record the handoff dates so the traceability from assessment to program change is examinable.
checklist.done: documented handoffs carry assessment conclusions into the WISP and the control baseline with dates.

checklist.step: Report results to the CISO and the board
actions: Present the assessment's top risks, remediation posture and open acceptances to the security governance committee.
Fold the assessment summary into the annual Section 4(e) board report and load it to the board portal for the Q4 sitting.
Capture any executive direction (accelerate a fix, fund a control) as tracked actions with owners.
checklist.done: assessment results are presented, board-reported and any directed actions are tracked.

checklist.step: Retain the assessment evidence set
actions: File the report, scoring workpapers, scan exports, pen-test report, remediation tickets extract and acceptance register under REG-052-C02/<year>.
Apply the 5-year retention label and verify retrieval by year and by finding id.
Restrict access to Security, Risk, Compliance and Internal Audit — the pen-test report especially.
checklist.done: the full assessment evidence set is filed, labelled 5 years and access-restricted.

checklist.step: Log assessment-process exceptions
actions: Raise a GRC exception for any process breach: assessment slipping past 12 months, a scope exclusion without rationale, or an SLA breach without acceptance.
Assign root cause and owner, and set a remediation date.
Report open exceptions to the security governance committee quarterly.
checklist.done: process breaches are individually logged with root cause, owner and date, and reported quarterly.

checklist.step: Close the cycle with CISO sign-off
actions: Review the closed-versus-open remediation ledger and the acceptance register at cycle end.
Sign the assessment-cycle closure memo stating the register is current and remediation is on-SLA or accepted.
Confirm the results are reflected in the certification support file for February 15.
File the signed memo in the evidence repository.
checklist.done: a signed closure memo confirms register currency, SLA posture and certification readiness.

testing.step: Build the population from the frozen risk register and remediation ledger
actions: Extract every risk row from the frozen assessment register in Archer and every remediation ticket opened from the assessment, with severities and dates.
Extract the scan and pen-test finding lists as independent sub-populations.
Record row counts and extraction dates in the workpaper as the population baseline.
testing.done: the register, ticket and finding populations are extracted with counts and dates baselined.

testing.step: Reconcile assessed coverage to the independent asset inventory
actions: Pull the CMDB list of systems holding nonpublic information as of the assessment scope date.
Match each CMDB system to a scored register row or a documented exclusion rationale.
Treat any unmatched, unrationalized system as an automatic exception — a silent scope gap defeats Section 4(c).
testing.done: every CMDB nonpublic-information system maps to a score or a rationale, with gaps listed as exceptions.

testing.step: Draw the documented sample
actions: Take 100% of critical findings, plus 25 risk rows selected at random (seeded, reproducible) across systems and threat classes, minimum 35 rows total.
Record the seed, population size and selection date so the sample can be re-drawn.
Include at least 5 rows that concluded 'safeguard sufficient' — sufficiency calls need testing as much as findings.
testing.done: a reproducible sample covers all criticals, a random cross-section and sufficiency conclusions.

testing.step: Re-perform the scoring on sampled rows
actions: For each sampled row, read the recorded rationale, then independently re-score likelihood and impact from the same inputs (SIEM statistics, data sensitivity, scan results) using the approved 5x5 methodology.
Compare to the recorded score; a deviation of more than one band in either dimension is an exception.
Note any row whose rationale is too thin to re-score — irreproducibility is itself a fail.
testing.done: every sampled row has an independent re-score within one band or a logged exception.

testing.step: Trace the technical evidence behind scans and the penetration test
actions: Open the scanner console and verify the scan jobs cited in the assessment ran in-period, authenticated, over the scoped asset groups.
Compare the scanner's own asset counts to the report's claimed coverage and investigate shortfalls.
Verify the penetration-test report is in-period, scoped to nonpublic-information systems, and that each pen-test finding appears in the remediation ledger.
testing.done: scan and pen-test evidence is verified at source and every finding traces into the ledger.

testing.step: Recompute remediation SLA maths
actions: For every critical and 15 sampled high/medium tickets, recompute due date = finding registration date + SLA days (30/90/180) and compare to the ticket's recorded due date.
Compare actual closure dates to due dates and list breaches.
For each breach, check whether a signed, countersigned risk acceptance existed before the due date — a breach without one is an exception; an acceptance signed after the fact is a worse one.
testing.done: SLA dates reconcile, and every breach is either covered by a pre-dated acceptance or logged as an exception.

testing.step: Verify closure evidence and retests
actions: For 15 sampled closed tickets, open the attached retest evidence (rescan result or re-performed exploit step) and confirm it post-dates the fix and shows the finding cleared.
Check the Archer residual score was updated after verification.
A ticket closed on the owner's say-so with no retest artifact is an exception.
testing.done: sampled closures carry dated retest artifacts and updated residual scores.

testing.step: Verify governance reporting of the assessment
actions: Confirm the assessment summary appears in the annual Section 4(e) board report on the board portal and that the security governance committee minutes record the results presentation.
Trace one board-directed action (if any) to a tracked, owned task.
Confirm the assessment completion date precedes the board report date — a report describing an unfinished assessment is an exception.
testing.done: board and committee records evidence timely reporting of completed assessment results.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one GRC issue per exception with the risk row or ticket id, what failed and the exposure.
Assign root cause (scope miss, scoring drift, SLA overrun, missing retest) and an owner with a date.
Flag to the CISO any exception that contradicts statements planned for the February 15 certification.
Carry open items into next year's test as mandatory retests.
testing.done: each exception carries root cause, owner, date, certification flag and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, sign and report the verification
actions: Compute the exception rate against the thresholds (stale assessment, silent scope gap, unaccepted SLA breach, irreproducible score all fail).
Write the conclusion — effective / effective with exceptions / ineffective — with workpaper references.
Sign as independent reviewer having scored no sampled row and owned no sampled ticket, and file the workpaper under REG-052-C02/<year>/test.
Report to the audit committee and copy the CISO before the certification cycle.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion is filed and reported ahead of certification.

checklist.step: Derive the annual control baseline from the risk assessment
actions: Take the safeguard-sufficiency conclusions from the completed risk assessment (REG-052-C02) and translate each into a concrete control requirement with a measurable standard (e.g. MFA on 100% of remote access, AES-256 at rest on all nonpublic-information stores).
Record the baseline in Archer with one row per control, its owning engineer and its evidence source.
Get CISO approval on the baseline and publish it to the security engineering teams.
Diff the new baseline against last year's and open implementation tickets for every new or tightened requirement.
checklist.done: a CISO-approved baseline with per-control owners and evidence sources is published, with tickets open for every delta.

checklist.step: Enforce MFA on all remote access to nonpublic information
actions: In the Okta Admin Console open Security ▸ Authentication Policies and verify every application tagged as holding nonpublic information sits behind a policy requiring MFA for any off-network sign-on.
Review Security ▸ Global Session Policy for exclusion rules and remove any legacy bypass (service accounts route to CyberArk instead, never to an MFA exemption).
Export the policy set to JSON monthly, date-stamp it and file it as configuration evidence.
Reconcile the Okta application list against the CMDB nonpublic-information inventory and enroll any unfederated application or raise a compensating-control exception.
checklist.done: every nonpublic-information application enforces MFA on remote sign-on, with a monthly dated policy export and a clean CMDB reconciliation.

checklist.step: Vault and rotate privileged credentials
actions: Maintain the privileged-account inventory in CyberArk covering domain admins, database admins on nonpublic-information stores, cloud root/owner accounts and break-glass credentials.
Enforce check-out with MFA, session recording on Tier 0 assets and automatic rotation after each use (or 30 days for service accounts).
Run the monthly unmanaged-privileged-account discovery scan and onboard or disable every hit within 10 business days.
Report vault coverage percentage in the monthly metrics pack.
checklist.done: privileged accounts are vaulted with MFA check-out and rotation, and discovery hits are dispositioned within 10 business days.

checklist.step: Maintain the encryption-at-rest inventory over nonpublic-information stores
actions: Keep a per-datastore inventory (databases, file shares, object storage, backups) recording the encryption state, algorithm and key ownership for every store holding nonpublic information.
Verify new stores enter the inventory through the architecture-review gate before production data lands.
Remediate or exception any unencrypted store within 30 days — backups and file shares are where this control usually fails.
Refresh the inventory quarterly and file the dated export in the evidence repository.
checklist.done: a quarterly-refreshed inventory shows every nonpublic-information store encrypted or under a dated exception.

checklist.step: Enforce encryption in transit on external and internal paths
actions: Scan external endpoints monthly for protocol grade and fail anything below TLS 1.2; track certificate expiry with 30-day alerts.
Verify internal service-to-service paths carrying nonpublic information (API gateway routes, database connections, SFTP feeds to third parties) enforce encryption per the standard.
Open remediation tickets for every weak-protocol finding with the standard patching SLA.
File the monthly scan summary as evidence.
checklist.done: monthly scans show no external endpoint below TLS 1.2 and internal nonpublic-information paths verified, with breaches ticketed.

checklist.step: Operate key management and rotation
actions: Maintain the key inventory (KMS keys, certificates, application secrets) with owner, rotation period and last-rotated date.
Rotate per the standard (annually for data keys, on personnel change for shared secrets) and log each rotation.
Restrict key-administration rights to the named key custodians and review the custodian list quarterly.
Escalate any key past its rotation date to the IT Security Manager weekly.
checklist.done: the key inventory shows every key within its rotation period or escalated, with a quarterly-reviewed custodian list.

checklist.step: Run the quarterly access recertification campaign
actions: In SailPoint open Certifications ▸ Campaigns and launch the quarterly campaign covering all entitlements on nonpublic-information applications plus all privileged roles.
Set the 30-day completion window with auto-reminders at day 14 and 21 and manager escalation at day 25.
Configure revocations to execute automatically on certifier decision and verify each revocation completed in the target system within 5 business days.
Export the campaign completion report (certifier decisions, revocations executed, non-responders) and file it; chase non-responder items to zero before campaign close.
checklist.done: the campaign closes within 30 days at 100% decisioned, revocations are verified executed and the report is filed.

checklist.step: Deprovision leavers within 24 hours
actions: Verify the Workday-to-SailPoint termination feed runs at least hourly and triggers automatic disablement of Okta SSO, VPN, email and application accounts on the termination effective timestamp.
For immediate/for-cause terminations, execute the manual kill-switch runbook within 1 hour of the HR call and record the timestamps.
Run the daily orphan report comparing active accounts to Workday active headcount and disable any account whose owner terminated more than 24 hours ago, then investigate why the feed missed it.
Log every 24-hour breach as a GRC exception with root cause.
checklist.done: the termination feed disables access on effective time, the daily orphan report runs clean and any breach is logged with root cause.

checklist.step: Maintain endpoint protection coverage
actions: In the Falcon console open Host setup and management ▸ Host management and reconcile enrolled sensor count against the CMDB endpoint population; investigate every unenrolled or stale (no check-in over 7 days) host.
Verify prevention policies are in enforce mode (not detect-only) on all server and workstation groups.
Route Falcon detections into Splunk so endpoint telemetry joins the audit trail.
Report coverage percentage and stale-host count in the monthly metrics pack.
checklist.done: sensor coverage reconciles to the CMDB, policies enforce, telemetry flows to Splunk and coverage is reported monthly.

checklist.step: Operate audit trails and security monitoring
actions: Verify the Splunk ingestion health dashboard shows log sources green for every nonpublic-information system (authentication, database audit, privileged session, network egress) and chase any silent source within 24 hours.
Tune and operate the detection rules for the Model 668 threat set: mass nonpublic-information export, impossible-travel sign-on, privileged use outside CyberArk, encryption-disable events.
Triage alerts per the SOC runbook and escalate suspected cybersecurity events to the Incident Response Lead (REG-052-C04) without delay — the 72-hour regulatory clock depends on prompt escalation.
Retain audit logs per the retention standard so investigations satisfy Section 5's five-year record duty.
checklist.done: log sources are green, detections operate against the defined threat set and escalation paths to IR are exercised and documented.

checklist.step: Run patching to SLA over the in-scope estate
actions: Publish the weekly severity-ranked patch list from the scanner to system owners with due dates computed from the SLA (critical 14 days, high 30 days).
Track burn-down on the SLA dashboard and escalate any critical past due to the IT Security Manager the same day.
Rescan patched assets to confirm closure before tickets close.
Report SLA compliance percentage in the monthly metrics pack; below 95% triggers a remediation plan.
checklist.done: patching runs to SLA with rescan-verified closures and monthly compliance reporting at or above 95% or under a plan.

checklist.step: Execute secure disposal of nonpublic information
actions: Apply the retention schedule so nonpublic information past its retention period is queued for disposal per Section 4(d)(2)'s secure-disposal safeguard.
For physical media, use the contracted destruction vendor and collect a certificate of destruction per batch listing media serials and method.
For logical deletion, run the disposal job with a completion log and spot-verify a sample of deleted identifiers cannot be retrieved.
File certificates and logs in the compliance evidence repository.
checklist.done: expired nonpublic information is destroyed with certificates or verified deletion logs on file.

checklist.step: Manage control exceptions with compensating controls
actions: Register any system unable to meet a baseline control (legacy platform without MFA support, unencryptable appliance) as an exception with the compensating control (network isolation, enhanced monitoring) documented.
Set an expiry of no more than 12 months and require IT Security Manager approval, with CISO approval where the gap touches consumer nonpublic information.
Review the exception register monthly and refuse silent renewals — each expiry is re-argued on current risk.
Surface the register in the certification support file so the February 15 certification reflects known gaps.
checklist.done: every baseline gap is a registered, approved, expiry-dated exception with a compensating control, reviewed monthly.

checklist.step: Publish monthly control metrics to the CISO
actions: Assemble the monthly pack: MFA coverage, vault coverage, certification campaign status, leaver-deprovisioning breaches, encryption inventory gaps, endpoint coverage, patching SLA and open exceptions.
Publish the Power BI dashboard to the CISO and the security governance committee with month-over-month trend.
Flag any metric breaching its threshold with the recovery action and owner.
Archive each month's pack in the evidence repository — the metrics trail is certification support.
checklist.done: a monthly metrics pack with thresholds, trends and recovery actions is published and archived.

checklist.step: Close control-failure remediations with CISO sign-off
actions: Review each closed control-failure remediation (MFA gap, leaver breach, unencrypted store) with the attached fix evidence.
Sign the closure or send it back with the residual concern named.
Direct any failure that exposed nonpublic information into the incident process (REG-052-C04) for a cybersecurity-event determination.
File signed closures in the evidence repository.
checklist.done: control-failure closures carry CISO signature and any exposure-bearing failure was routed to incident determination.

testing.step: Build the system and identity populations
actions: Extract the CMDB list of systems holding nonpublic information, the Okta application list, the SailPoint entitlement catalog and the year's Workday leaver list with termination timestamps.
Record counts and extraction dates as the population baseline.
Note the four quarterly certification campaigns and the twelve monthly metrics packs as document sub-populations.
testing.done: system, identity, leaver and document populations are extracted with counts and dates.

testing.step: Reconcile the control scope across sources
actions: Match every CMDB nonpublic-information system to an Okta MFA-protected application, a SailPoint-governed entitlement set and an encryption-inventory row.
List systems missing from any of the three as scope gaps.
Treat a nonpublic-information system absent from MFA or certification scope as an automatic exception.
testing.done: every in-scope system reconciles across MFA, certification and encryption scopes or is listed as an exception.

testing.step: Draw the documented samples
actions: Select 25 systems at random (seeded, reproducible) plus all Tier 0/privileged platforms; select 20 leavers at random from the year including at least 3 for-cause terminations; select 2 of the 4 certification campaigns.
Record seeds, population sizes and selection dates in the workpaper.
Keep the samples independent of any system the auditor administers.
testing.done: reproducible system, leaver and campaign samples are drawn and documented.

testing.step: Re-perform the MFA policy check in Okta
actions: With read-only access, open Security ▸ Authentication Policies for each sampled application and independently confirm an MFA requirement applies to off-network sign-on with no exclusion rules.
Compare the live policy to the month's filed JSON export to prove the evidence trail matches reality.
Query the sign-on log for each sampled application for the last 30 days and verify no successful remote authentication bypassed MFA.
Any bypass path or export mismatch is an exception.
testing.done: sampled applications show live MFA enforcement matching filed exports, with sign-on logs free of bypasses.

testing.step: Trace leaver deprovisioning to the 24-hour standard
actions: For each sampled leaver, compare the Workday termination effective timestamp to the SailPoint/Okta disablement timestamps and compute the elapsed hours.
For the for-cause sample, verify the 1-hour kill-switch runbook timestamps.
Search the sampled leavers' accounts for any authentication event after termination in the Splunk sign-on logs.
Any access surviving 24 hours, or any post-termination authentication, is an exception.
testing.done: every sampled leaver shows disablement within standard and zero post-termination authentications.

testing.step: Re-perform the certification campaign checks
actions: For the two sampled campaigns, verify launch and close dates sit within the 30-day window and completion reached 100% of decisioned items.
Sample 15 revocation decisions per campaign and confirm each revoked entitlement is genuinely absent from the target system today.
Check certifiers were the access owners' managers or application owners, not the IAM team certifying itself.
A revocation still live in the target system is an exception regardless of the campaign report.
testing.done: sampled campaigns closed on time at full completion and sampled revocations verifiably executed.

testing.step: Verify encryption at rest on sampled stores
actions: For 10 sampled datastores from the encryption inventory (including at least 2 backup targets and 1 file share), obtain a current configuration capture from the platform console showing encryption enabled and the algorithm.
Compare the capture to the inventory row; verify key ownership matches the custodian list.
For any store under exception, verify the compensating control (isolation, monitoring) is actually configured.
An unencrypted store outside a dated exception is an automatic exception at critical severity.
testing.done: sampled stores show console-evidenced encryption matching the inventory, with exceptions' compensating controls verified.

testing.step: Recompute patching and coverage SLA maths
actions: From the raw scanner data, recompute the quarter's patching SLA compliance for criticals (14 days) and highs (30 days) and compare to the reported figures in the monthly metrics packs.
Recompute endpoint coverage from Falcon host counts against the CMDB and compare to the reported percentage.
A reported metric that cannot be reproduced within 2 percentage points from source data is an exception.
testing.done: reported SLA and coverage metrics are reproduced from source data within tolerance.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one GRC issue per exception naming the system or identity, the control that failed and the nonpublic-information exposure.
Assign root cause (scope gap, feed failure, config drift, metric misstatement) and an owner with a remediation date.
Route any exception indicating actual unauthorized access to the Incident Response Lead for a cybersecurity-event determination under REG-052-C04.
Carry open exceptions into the next quarterly spot-check as mandatory retests.
testing.done: each exception is tracked with root cause, owner and date, and access-indicating items routed to incident determination.

testing.step: Conclude, sign and report the control test
actions: Compute results against the thresholds (any MFA gap, 24-hour leaver breach, late campaign, unencrypted store or sub-95% patching fails).
Write the conclusion — effective / effective with exceptions / ineffective — with workpaper references and the quarter-by-quarter spot-check results appended.
Sign as independent reviewer holding no administrative access to the tested platforms, and file under REG-052-C03/<year>/test.
Report to the audit committee and copy the CISO ahead of the February 15 certification.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion is filed and reported before certification.

checklist.step: Maintain the IR plan with every Section 4(h) required element
actions: Keep the IR plan current in the SharePoint policy library covering the Section 4(h) elements: internal response process, clear roles and decision authority, external and internal communication plans, remediation of identified weaknesses, documentation of events and responses, regulatory reporting duties and post-event plan revision.
Cross-reference the state notification matrix and the Section 6(b) content template as controlled appendices.
Re-approve the plan annually with the CISO and after every material event.
Distribute the on-call roster and escalation tree to the SOC and verify contact details quarterly.
checklist.done: a current, CISO-approved plan covers all Section 4(h) elements with live appendices and a verified escalation tree.

checklist.step: Define the cybersecurity-event determination standard
actions: Write the determination standard from the model definition: an event resulting in unauthorized access to, or disruption or misuse of, an information system or the nonpublic information stored on it — noting the exclusions (encrypted data without the key; events where no nonpublic information was used or its return is assured).

Name the determination authority (CISO or delegate with counsel consult) and require a written, timestamped determination memo for every escalated incident, including 'not a cybersecurity event' conclusions.
Train the SOC and IR teams on the standard annually so escalation is fast and consistent.
State explicitly in the standard that the 72-hour clock starts at the determination timestamp, and that determination must not be artificially delayed.
checklist.done: a counsel-authored standard with named authority, mandatory timestamped memos and clock-start rules is in force and trained.

checklist.step: Run the annual tabletop exercise against the plan
actions: Design a scenario touching nonpublic information (e.g. ransomware with exfiltration across multiple states) and run the tabletop with SOC, IT, Legal, Compliance, Privacy and Communications at the table.
Exercise the full chain: detection, determination memo, 72-hour clock computation, state-matrix lookup, draft commissioner notification and consumer-notice decision.
Document findings and lessons with owners and due dates, and track them to closure in the ITSM tracker.
File the exercise report in the evidence repository — the annual test is itself examinable evidence.
checklist.done: an annual tabletop exercised the full determination-to-notification chain with a filed report and tracked findings.

checklist.step: Triage security alerts into incident tickets without gaps
actions: Work the Splunk alert queue per the SOC runbook and open a ServiceNow security-incident ticket for every alert meeting the triage threshold, linking the alert id.
Apply the severity matrix and escalate any incident with possible nonpublic-information involvement to the Incident Response Lead within 1 hour.
Never close a high-severity alert without either a ticket or a documented false-positive rationale.
Review the alert-to-ticket reconciliation weekly with the SOC Lead.
checklist.done: every threshold alert has a ticket or a documented false-positive call, and possible-nonpublic-information incidents escalate within 1 hour.

checklist.step: Investigate per Section 5 and preserve forensic evidence
actions: For each escalated incident, promptly determine per Section 5(b): whether a cybersecurity event occurred, its nature and scope, the nonpublic information involved, and perform reasonable measures to restore system security.
Collect forensic images and Falcon telemetry under chain-of-custody, and preserve logs beyond normal rotation for the affected window.
Record the affected consumer count by state — this drives which of the 44 jurisdictions' notification thresholds trigger.
Write the investigation report into the incident ticket with evidence references.
checklist.done: each escalated incident has a Section 5 investigation report with preserved evidence and a per-state affected-consumer count.

checklist.step: Make the determination and start the 72-hour clock
actions: Convene the CISO and Regulatory Counsel as soon as the investigation supports a conclusion, and record the determination (cybersecurity event / not an event) in a memo with the exact date-time.
Enter the determination timestamp into the ServiceNow security-incident record so the 72-hour deadline auto-computes and the T-48/T-24/T-6 alerts arm.
Notify the Compliance Manager and Privacy Officer the same hour so consumer-notice analysis starts in parallel.
For 'not an event' conclusions, file the memo anyway — the negative determinations are the first thing an examiner samples.
checklist.done: a timestamped determination memo exists, the 72-hour countdown is armed in ServiceNow and Compliance and Privacy are engaged.

checklist.step: Run the state notification matrix for the event
actions: Open the variance appendix and mark: the domiciliary state commissioner (notification required regardless of consumer count in most adoptions) and each other adopting state where the trigger is met (commonly 250 or more affected consumers resident in the state plus a notice obligation under other law, or reasonable likelihood of material harm).
Record the per-state window from the appendix — 72 hours is the model, but confirm each state's enacted figure rather than assuming.
List each state's delivery channel (DOI cybersecurity-event web form, designated email, or written filing) with the address from the appendix.
Have Regulatory Counsel confirm the final state list in writing before drafting begins.
checklist.done: a counsel-confirmed state list exists with per-state window, trigger basis and delivery channel.

checklist.step: Draft the commissioner notification with the Section 6(b) content
actions: Complete the content template covering the Section 6(b) items: date of the event, description of how the information was exposed or compromised, how the event was discovered, whether lost or stolen information has been recovered, the identity of the source of the event if known, whether law enforcement was notified, the types of nonpublic information involved, the period during which the system was compromised, the number of consumers affected in that state, the results of any internal review, remediation efforts, a copy of the licensee's privacy policy and the contact for further information.
Mark unknown items as 'under investigation — supplement to follow' rather than omitting them; the model act contemplates ongoing supplementation as facts develop.
Tailor the consumer count and any state-specific fields per state from the matrix.
Route the draft to the CISO for factual sign-off and the General Counsel for privilege review before submission.
checklist.done: a per-state notification draft covers every Section 6(b) item or flags it for supplementation, with CISO and GC sign-off.

checklist.step: Submit to every required commissioner inside the window
actions: Submit each state's notification through its recorded channel — the state DOI's cybersecurity-event reporting form or designated email — before the deadline computed from the determination timestamp.
Capture proof per state: web-form confirmation number, email delivery receipt or certified-mail tracking, and log each into the regulatory tracker against the incident id.
Where facts are still developing, send the compliant initial notice on time and diarise the supplement rather than holding for completeness.
Report submission status to the CISO at each ServiceNow alert checkpoint until all states show submitted.
checklist.done: every required state shows a logged submission with proof, timestamped inside its window.

checklist.step: Execute consumer notification under each state's breach statute
actions: Determine consumer-notice obligations per affected state's general data-breach statute (which Model 668 Section 6(c) defers to), including timing, content and attorney-general copies.
Engage the mail/notification vendor, seed the consumer file from the investigation's affected-consumer list and proofread the notice against each state's content requirements.
Offer credit monitoring where statute or company policy requires and stand up the call-center script with the Contact Center Ops Manager.
File notice proofs (mailing certification, sample letters) against the incident id.
checklist.done: consumer notices meet each state's breach statute with proofs filed and support channels live.

checklist.step: Notify producers of record where the adoption requires
actions: For states whose adoption carries the producer-of-record notice (Section 6(f)), extract the producers of record for affected consumers from the producer management system.
Issue the notice within the state's timing using the counsel-approved template, excluding producers whose authority has lapsed per the state's carve-out.
Log delivery per producer against the incident id.
Field producer questions through the Agency Relations team with the approved FAQ.
checklist.done: producers of record in triggering states are notified on time with logged delivery.

checklist.step: Handle reinsurance and third-party event paths
actions: Where the company acts as assuming reinsurer and the event involves ceding-insurer data, notify each affected ceding insurer within 72 hours of determination per Section 6(e), with the same content discipline.

Where the event occurred at a third-party service provider, confirm the TPSP intake (REG-052-C06) delivered the vendor's facts, and treat the licensee's own determination and notification duties as running on the licensee's clock, not the vendor's.
Log cross-party notifications and receipts against the incident id.
Brief Regulatory Counsel on any counterparty dispute over notification responsibility.
checklist.done: ceding insurers and third-party paths are handled inside 72 hours with logged notices and counsel visibility.

checklist.step: Retain the complete investigation record for 5 years
actions: Assemble the event file: investigation report, forensic evidence index, determination memo, state matrix run, all notifications with proofs, consumer and producer notice records and the post-incident review.
File it in the compliance evidence repository under the incident id with a 5-year retention label per Section 5(c).
Restrict access to Security, Legal, Compliance and Internal Audit given the confidentiality provisions around Section 6 material.
Verify retrieval by incident id and by state.
checklist.done: a complete event file is retained 5 years, access-restricted and retrievable by incident id and state.

checklist.step: Run the post-incident review and update the plan
actions: Within 30 days of event closure, hold the post-incident review covering detection speed, determination latency, notification timeliness and control failures.
Open remediation items for every weakness with owners and dates, and route control gaps into the REG-052-C03 baseline.
Amend the IR plan and the state matrix where the event exposed procedural gaps, re-approving through the CISO.
Feed the event summary into the annual Section 4(e) board report.
checklist.done: a 30-day post-incident review produced tracked remediations, plan updates and board-report input.

checklist.step: Log notification breaches and close with sign-off
actions: Log any late or missed notification (state, consumer, producer, ceding insurer) as a regulatory exception with the overrun hours and root cause.
Have Regulatory Counsel assess self-report posture and any curative filing to the affected commissioner.
Obtain CISO signature on the remediation closure and counsel countersignature on notification-breach closures.
Carry the breach pattern into the next tabletop scenario.
checklist.done: every breach is logged, counsel-assessed, remediated under dual sign-off and reflected in the next exercise.

testing.step: Build the incident population for the trailing 12 months
actions: Extract every security-incident ticket opened in ServiceNow in the period with severity, timestamps and determination outcome.
Extract the SIEM high-severity alert log for the same period as the independent completeness source.
Pull the annual tabletop record and the IR plan approval history as document sub-populations.
Baseline the counts and extraction dates in the workpaper.
testing.done: ticket, alert and document populations are extracted and baselined.

testing.step: Reconcile alerts to tickets so no event escaped the pipeline
actions: Match every high-severity Splunk alert to a ServiceNow ticket or a documented false-positive rationale.
Investigate unmatched alerts with the SOC Lead and treat any unticketed true alert as an automatic exception — a missed alert is a missed clock.
Check weekly SOC reconciliation reviews actually ran by sampling 4 weeks of review records.
testing.done: every high-severity alert maps to a ticket or rationale, with unmatched true alerts logged as exceptions.

testing.step: Select the event sample
actions: Take 100% of determined cybersecurity events (these are rare and each carries regulatory exposure) plus 15 randomly selected (seeded, reproducible) escalated incidents concluded 'not an event'.
Record the seed, population and selection date.
Include any event originating at a third-party service provider so the TPSP intake path is covered.
testing.done: all determined events and a reproducible negative-determination sample are selected.

testing.step: Re-perform the determination judgement on sampled incidents
actions: For each sampled incident, read the investigation report first and independently apply the determination standard — unauthorized access, disruption or misuse of systems or nonpublic information, minus the encryption and no-use exclusions — before reading the recorded memo.
Compare conclusions; a 'not an event' call the auditor would have determined as an event is a critical exception.
Check every sampled incident has a written, timestamped memo signed by the named authority — an undocumented determination fails even if the call was right.
Verify determination latency: flag any incident where the memo post-dates investigation-support by more than 5 business days as possible clock management.
testing.done: each sampled incident carries an independent re-determination, a verified memo and a latency check.

testing.step: Recompute the 72-hour maths on every determined event
actions: For each determined event and each required state, compute elapsed hours from the determination timestamp to the logged submission proof timestamp.
Compare against that state's enacted window from the variance appendix, re-verifying the appendix figure against current statute for each state touched.
Any submission past its window is an automatic exception at critical severity; any required state absent from the submission log is worse.
Verify the ServiceNow countdown alerts actually fired by inspecting the notification log.
testing.done: every state submission recomputes inside its enacted window or is logged as a critical exception.

testing.step: Trace notification content to the Section 6(b) checklist
actions: For each state submission, tick the notification against the Section 6(b) content items — event date, exposure description, discovery method, recovery status, source identity, law-enforcement status, nonpublic-information types, compromise period, per-state consumer count, internal-review results, remediation, privacy policy and contact.
Confirm items marked 'under investigation' were followed by a logged supplement once facts landed.
Verify CISO factual sign-off and General Counsel review pre-date each submission.
A missing content item with no supplement is an exception.
testing.done: each submission evidences full Section 6(b) content or logged supplements, with pre-submission sign-offs.

testing.step: Verify consumer, producer and ceding-insurer notice execution
actions: For each determined event, trace consumer notices to mailing certifications and state breach-statute timing, sampling 10 consumer records against the investigation's affected list.
Trace producer-of-record notices in triggering states to delivery logs in the producer management system.
Where the company assumed reinsurance, verify ceding-insurer notices inside 72 hours with receipts.
Any affected consumer absent from the notice file is an exception.
testing.done: consumer, producer and ceding-insurer notices trace to proofs consistent with the affected population.

testing.step: Verify the annual plan test and 5-year record retention
actions: Confirm the tabletop exercise ran within the last 12 months, exercised the determination-to-notification chain, and its findings are tracked to closure.
Sample the event files in the compliance evidence repository and confirm each carries the 5-year retention label and retrieves complete by incident id.
Confirm access restrictions on Section 6 material are in force by attempting retrieval with a non-privileged test account.
A missing tabletop year or an incomplete event file is an exception.
testing.done: the annual test, retention labels, file completeness and access restrictions are all evidenced.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one tracker issue per exception with the incident id, state, what failed and the regulatory exposure.
Assign root cause (missed alert, delayed determination, matrix error, content gap, late supplement) and an owner with a date.
For any late or missed commissioner notification, open a self-report assessment with Regulatory Counsel immediately.
Carry open exceptions into the next tabletop and the next annual test.
testing.done: every exception is tracked with root cause and owner, and notification breaches carry a counsel self-report assessment.

testing.step: Conclude, sign and report the IR verification
actions: Compute results against the zero-tolerance thresholds (any late commissioner notification, unticketed true alert, undocumented determination or skipped tabletop fails).
Write the conclusion — effective / effective with exceptions / ineffective — with workpaper references per event.
Sign as independent reviewer having served in no reviewed incident command, and file under REG-052-C04/<year>/test.
Report to the audit committee and the CISO, and flag any conclusion that must be reflected in the February 15 certification.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion and certification flag is filed and reported.
